1.pericope_label: Son of man, thou dwellest in the midst of a rebellious house, which have eyes to see, and see not; they have ears to hear, and hear not: for they are a rebellious house
debates: Why the prophet is warned of their obstinacy before being commanded
What the stuff for removing includes
outliers: Calvin gives two reasons for the warning, to give the prophet fortitude against the temptation of speaking to the deaf, and to forestall his objecting that the sign would look ridiculous
Clarke holds it is not want of grace that destroys them but the abuse of grace they had, since no man is lost for want of sufficient grace
Ellicott reconstructs the action precisely, the goods carried out through the day and the prophet leaving only at evening, as one who saves what he can before abandoning his home
Keil and Delitzsch place the section within the eleven months between two dated visions, on the ground of its contents rather than any date
themes: A legal fiction of going out to view a disputed field
Faith by hearing called more sure than vision
A performance derided as a boyish amusement
Garments called vessels by the Latins

4.pericope_label: Dig thou through the wall in their sight, and carry out thereby. In their sight shalt thou bear it upon thy shoulders, and carry it forth in the twilight
debates: Whether the question of the people was sincere or derisive
What the covering of the face signifies
Who is carried on whose shoulders
outliers: Calvin argues from the repeated epithet rebellious that the question was derision, since God would not have called them so had it proceeded from mere folly
Ellicott takes the morning message as evidence that the symbolic action was actually performed, the divine word coming in answer to their inquiry
Clarke conjectures that the covered face points to the king being carried in a palanquin with a cloth over his eyes because of the recent wounds
Gill reports two ancient versions that reverse the clause so that the prophet is carried on the shoulders of another, and prefers the plainer sense
themes: A wall of sun-dried brick easily dug through
Docility required before a question may be asked
Escape by night compared to the work of thieves
A word for twilight used only three times and rendered dark

12.pericope_label: My net also will I spread upon him, and he shall be taken in my snare: and I will bring him to Babylon to the land of the Chaldeans; yet shall he not see it, though he shall die there
debates: Whether the remnant left are the faithful
How the king could be brought to Babylon and not see it
Whether the digging through the wall is literal
outliers: Calvin argues against the reading that makes the survivors the faithful preserved in the midst of death, holding the passage speaks of the people in general and that they are left as witnesses rather than in mercy
Ellicott and Clarke both explain the not seeing by the putting out of the eyes of the king before he was carried away
Ellicott holds the digging need not be figurative, since a breach at an unwatched place could be arranged for secrecy and passed over in a brief narrative
Calvin takes the net as God claiming for himself what the Chaldeans executed, since without his provision all their endeavours would have been fruitless
themes: A netman and a pursuer described from ancient combat
A king disbelieving two prophecies because he thought them contradictory
A play on words between men of number and recounting
The dispersion of sinners said to prove the dispersion of penitents

17.pericope_label: Son of man, eat thy bread with quaking, and drink thy water with trembling and with carefulness
debates: Who the people of the land are
Whether the sign was actually performed
Whether the bread and water imply scanty provision
outliers: Gill, Calvin and Ellicott take the people of the land for the exiles in Chaldea, while Wesley divides the phrase and reads the land as the countries round about Jerusalem
Keil and Delitzsch hold the carrying out of the sign is simply taken for granted rather than doubtful
Keil and Delitzsch deny that scanty provision is to be sought in the words, bread and water being the standing expression for food
Henry insists the prophet was not dissembling but genuinely affected with grief at what he foretold
themes: A man bearing himself as one who has got an ague upon him
Ministers told to speak feelingly as those that know the terrors of the Lord
A suggestion that the prophecies were exchanged between the two lands
God compelling men to feel him when he is silent and executing

21.pericope_label: Son of man, what is that proverb that ye have in the land of Israel, saying, The days are prolonged, and every vision faileth?
debates: How the threatened days can be called near
What the promise to speak refers to
outliers: Ellicott holds the proverb was current among those not yet carried into captivity, who fancied that they should not be, rather than among the exiles
Calvin explains the nearness as spoken after the manner of men, since those then alive would see the accomplishment even after thirty years
Wesley reads the promise to speak of a continuing succession of ministers to the end of the world, where Gill and Calvin take it of the immediate word being performed
Calvin holds the false prophets were not removed but silenced, their mouth stopped when the event proved their wickedness
themes: A people more frightened than hurt refusing to trust a prophet again
The patience of God turned into material for obduracy
The very means used to bring sinners to repentance made the instruments of their destruction
The word of God seeming cold and dissipated into air unless the hand is considered

26.pericope_label: Therefore say unto them, Thus saith the Lord GOD; There shall none of my words be prolonged any more, but the word which I have spoken shall be done, saith the Lord GOD
debates: Who the house of Israel here are
How the clause about words not being prolonged should be construed
Whether this saying differs in kind from the earlier proverb
outliers: Gill leaves it open whether those speaking are the ten tribes in Babylon or the Jews in Judea
Calvin records a construction that changes the number, making each word severally not put off, but prefers the plainer reading as suiting the context
Calvin holds this second saying is oblique ridicule rather than the open blasphemy condemned earlier, though the one glides easily into the other
themes: Men granting the threat may come true and resolving to feast securely meanwhile
A prophet spending his strength in vain summoning by a loud trumpet
Mockers told they would live to see and feel the desolation
